title: 2025-05-07 Quantization Technical Review - Zenith AI

transcript:
Header: 2025-05-07 15:00 UTC | Duration: 53m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Samira Khan (Redwood AE), Diego Morales (Redwood SE), Asha Patel (Zenith Head ML Infra), Markus Lind (Zenith SRE), Priya Nair (Zenith ML Eng)

Summary (auto): quick bullets exchanged on INT8/FP8/GPTQ/AWQ pros/cons, KV cache interactions and plan for on-prem/VPC pilot.

[00:00] Samira: okay good afternoon everyone, thanks for joining, this is Samira from Redwood, with Diego our systems SE. we wanted to run through the quantization findings you sent and go over tradeoffs, yes?
[00:15] Asha: yep, thanks. Our main ask is we need to get to a 2-3x cost reduction on inference with less than 1.5% absolute latency on quality for our summarization model. we've seen some cracks with GPTQ where rouge drops more than expected.
[00:32] Diego: right, so quick framing — we typically look at three families: INT8 (post training / calibration), FP8 where available on hardware, and algorithmic approaches like GPTQ and AWQ (approx weight quant). they each have different perf/quality footprints.
[00:50] Markus: quick q, when you say AWQ, sometimes we saw it spelled AW-G or AW-Q in notes, are those the same?
[00:58] Diego: yeah sorry transcription artifact; AWQ here refers to the newer asymmetric weight quant methods — community impls vary and names differ. key thing is AWQ tends to keep accuracy better at low bit widths than naive symmetric INT8 in a lot of LLMs.
[01:12] Priya: our bench on GPTQ showed 2.8% f1 drop on entity extraction for the 13B model, which was painful.
[01:20] Diego: that aligns with other reports. GPTQ aims for per-channel reconstruction but can introduce layerwise noise that impacts generation-based metrics. AWQ and some FP8 flows are gentler, but hardware support for FP8 is limited unless you're on recent HW or simulation.
[01:40] Samira: also note that INT8 runtime paths on Redwood are highly optimized — we do kernel selection, and for some backends we use quantized GEMM kernels plus KV-cache-aware ops to reduce perf overhead. but accuracy varies by model and calibration set.
[01:59] Asha: can you say more about KV cache and quantization? our trouble seems to exacerbate when the model uses long context caching.
[02:08] Diego: sure — two things: first KV cache stores past keys/values unquantized in most setups; when you quantize weights but keep kv cache in fp16, mismatch can cause subtle distribution shifts on attention outputs. second, when using quantized memory layouts, some runtimes pack kv in lower precision to save memory; that can widen regressions.
[02:30] Markus: so is the recommendation to keep KV cache at fp16 and quantize just the weight matmuls?
[02:36] Diego: generally yes for first pass — keep kv fp16, quantize weights. some AWQ flows attempt quantized KV too but require careful calibration.
[02:48] Priya: what about batching tradeoffs? we need throughput spikes for peek loads.
[02:53] Diego: batching is a lever — more batch = better throughput but higher tail latency. on quantized runtimes batching also changes the memory layout and kernel path, so it can slightly affect output ordering and timing, but not accuracy if kernels are deterministic. the real issue is dynamic batching vs static. static larger batches can increase effective throughput.
[03:12] Asha: hardware question — we run on A6000s in our private infra, will FP8 kernels help there?
[03:18] Diego: A6000 doesn't have native FP8. FP8 benefits are mostly on newer Ampere/Next-gen hardware with transformer-optimized FP8 kernels; without native support FP8 is simulated and carries overhead. INT8 is more broadly useful on many GPUs with optimized int8 kernels.
[03:35] Samira: to add, Redwood's compiler will pick int8 kernels when beneficial; if FP8 is simulated the runtime often prefers fp16/INT8 hybrid.
[03:42] Markus: we heard Redwood has prefix KV caching to speed repeated prompts; does quantization break that?
[03:48] Diego: prefix caching (we call it prefix or prefix-KV) stores decoded prefixes and reused hidden states. Quantization may change hidden state distributions slightly if activation quantization is applied — that's why we recommend keeping activations in fp16 for prefix caches.
[04:05] Priya: any measurable numbers on throughput gains? our target ROI is 2-3x.
[04:10] Diego: rough rules: INT8 often gives 1.6x–2.2x token throughput vs fp16 depending on kernel maturity. AWQ/GPTQ at 4-bit or 3-bit can push 2.5x–3.5x but with higher risk of accuracy drop. FP8 if natively supported can approach similar to fp16 but with memory savings and modest perf gains. these are coarse.
[04:31] Asha: what about accuracy regression mitigation? we need to keep rouge/bleu within tight bounds.
[04:36] Diego: mitigation strategies: careful calibration set selection, per-layer rounding strategies, residual compensation, and selective dequantization of sensitive layers (eg first or last layers in transformer). AWQ tends to perform well with selective dequantization. also ensemble evals on your representative prompts.
[04:55] Samira: one approach we use is a delta-eval harness: run the same prompts across fp16 baseline, int8, awq(gptq) and compute per-prompt deltas and fallback thresholds. Redwood can automate rollback to fp16 for flagged prompts.
[05:12] Markus: about rollout — we need Canary rules and auto-fallback. can Redwood do per-prompt fallback?
[05:18] Samira: yes, we have rollout controls. we can route a small % to quantized variant and keep the rest on baseline; if quality metrics exceed threshold, traffic can failover. per-prompt fallback is more advanced but possible with our tracing hooks.
[05:34] Priya: we noticed when using GPTQ the first 50 tokens looked okay but later tokens showed drifting hallucinations. is that a known pattern?
[05:43] Diego: yes, drift can occur when quantization error compounds over autoregressive steps, especially with long contexts. keeping kv higher precision and limiting activation quantization helps. also sometimes reordering ffn/attn precision reduces drift.
[06:00] Asha: can you walk through a concrete experiment we'd run for us?
[06:04] Diego: sure — step 1: baseline runs with fp16 on your dev VPC for representative workloads (we need traces). step 2: generate quantized variants: INT8 calibrated, GPTQ, AWQ 4-bit. step 3: run token-level and holistic metric evaluations (rouge, f1, perplexity) and latency/throughput. step 4: analyze per-prompt deltas and identify sensitive prompts. step 5: build rollout plan with Canary thresholds.
[06:33] Priya: for GPTQ do you recommend per-layer nbits or global?
[06:37] Diego: per-layer is better — some layers are more sensitive. GPTQ implementations often support per-layer bitwidths; AWQ too. the heuristic is keep first attention and output projection higher precision.
[06:49] Samira: i will note that GPTQ has fast quantization time but sometimes optimization objective doesn't align with your downstream metric, so reconciling requires your evals.
[06:58] Markus: about memory — our primary constraint is kv memory for long convo histories. quantization helps but you said keep kv fp16...
[07:06] Diego: right — biggest memory wins come from quantizing weights (model weights on disk/memory) and possibly activations during inference; kv is tricky. an approach is delta-compressing kv or using offloading to CPU with compressed storage. Redwood supports compressed kv offload as an experimental path.
[07:24] Asha: any gotchas with multi-tenant Dedicated vs Private? we'll likely go private on prem later.
[07:30] Samira: Private/VPC differences: on-prem may limit kernel choices (older CUDA), so the runtime may not pick the latest int8 kernels and could fall back to fp16 sim paths. we usually run a compatibility matrix during onboarding. Dedicated (Redwood managed) gives us more control to tune kernels.
[07:48] Priya: ok, can you give example delta numbers from similar customers?
[07:52] Diego: sure — a fintech customer with a 13B model saw INT8 + selective dequant gave 1.9x throughput with 0.6% rouge drop; AWQ 4-bit gave 2.8x but 1.8% rouge drop until we selectively kept last two layers at fp16 which brought drop to 0.9%. results vary per model.
[08:12] Asha: that seems promising. where does GPTQ sit?
[08:15] Diego: GPTQ was in between for that customer: 2.4x throughput and ~1.1% rouge drop out of the box, but some prompt categories suffered more.
[08:25] Samira: quick aside — tools: we can share a spreadsheet with per-prompt deltas, and a benchmarking harness you can run in your VPC.
[08:33] Priya: yes please. also questions about our CI: we want quant artifacts to be part of model CI.
[08:38] Diego: good plan — version quantized artifacts and run nightly delta-evals. Redwood supports artifact versioning and model rollbacks.
[08:46] Markus: let's talk about fidelity: do you do stochastic rounding? I've read it can help.
[08:52] Diego: stochastic rounding can reduce bias in low-bit quant but adds nondeterminism. it helps in training-time quant, less common in inference due to reproducibility needs. deterministic methods with calibration often preferred for production.
[09:08] Asha: okay, what about FP8? you said hardware dependent — is it worth investing?
[09:13] Diego: FP8 is promising — less accuracy loss vs 8-bit ints in some cases and good memory savings. but until you have HW support it's simulation overhead. for Zenith on A6000s it's not worth it; if you plan to move to newer HW in 6-12 months then we can pipeline FP8 experiments.
[09:30] Priya: are there toolchains you recommend for GPTQ/AWQ? we've used bitsandbytes and some community scripts.
[09:37] Diego: bitsandbytes is common for int8; for GPTQ there are a couple community implementations (gptq-for-llm variants) and AWQ has some newer repos with community patches. Redwood's model onboarding team also has vetted conversion scripts we can share.
[09:52] Samira: we'll include links in the follow-up.
[09:55] Asha: let's cover perf testing specifics — what traces do you need?
[10:00] Diego: ideal: representative prompt set (1000–5000 prompts), distribution of lengths, token-level ground truth where possible, and a short set of heavy multi-turn sessions for drift testing. also request CPU/GPU specs, driver versions.
[10:18] Priya: we'll assemble that. any constraints on secrets/data? some prompts contain PII.
[10:23] Samira: we support VPC/on-prem testing precisely for that — you can run tests in your environment and share only metrics. Redwood can also sign an NDA and we have SOC2 artifacts.
[10:34] Markus: on metrics, you mentioned token-level traces. how do we correlate latency outliers with model deltas?
[10:39] Diego: we attach tracing IDs to prompts; latency histogram + token-level logits and outputs let us correlate deviance. Redwood tracing hooks can capture kernel paths used which helps isolate quantized kernel-induced outliers.
[10:54] Asha: ok, let's move to a quick Q/A: what are top 3 risks?
[10:59] Diego: 1) quality regressions on edge prompts, 2) unexpected drift with long contexts, 3) hardware/kernel incompatibilities in your on-prem stack.
[11:10] Priya: mitigation tactics?
[11:12] Diego: for 1) delta-eval + selective dequant, 2) preserve kv precision + early stopping if drift detected, 3) compatibility matrix and fallbacks to fp16.
[11:24] Samira: maybe a short demo of the benchmark sheet now? but given time maybe we keep to action items.
[11:30] Asha: fine. quick follow-ups: are there licensing implications for AWQ/GPTQ code? we can't have exported restricted code.
[11:38] Diego: community licenses vary; we can vet usage and prepare legal notes. we also offer managed conversion to avoid shipping code.
[11:47] Markus: anything special for k8s deployment on-prem?
[11:50] Diego: ensure drivers and cuda toolkit match the kernel expectations; container image we provide is tuned but you might have to allow certain nvidia driver levels. also ulimits for shm can impact large-kv workloads.
[12:05] Priya: ok noted.
[12:08] [long silence / typing]
[12:30] Samira: a couple of more technical points: quantization-aware quantization vs post-training? most infers use post-training with calibration but QAT during finetune helps if you can afford that.
[12:46] Diego: QAT usually gives the best results but requires retrain or fine-tune. if you can't retrain, GPTQ/AWQ or int8 post-calibration are the pragmatic paths.
[12:59] Asha: what about redwood runtime flags we should be aware of?
[13:03] Samira: we'll include config samples — e.g., force_kv_fp16=true, per_layer_dequant_list=[layer1,layerN], batching_defaults.
[13:15] Priya: you mentioned rollback thresholds: are those token-level or aggregate metrics?
[13:20] Diego: both — we support aggregate metric thresholds and per-prompt delta alerts.
[13:28] Asha: okay good.
[13:30] [FAST FORWARD: mid-call deeper dive] 
[25:00] Diego: walking through a sample trace: here's a prompt with long context, baseline fp16 produces stable tokens, INT8 variant's attention scores differ slightly at layer 10 leading to a changed token at t+70; that's the compound drift.
[25:24] Markus: can we instrument that layer in production?
[25:28] Diego: yes via our tracing hooks and layer-level comparators. we can return per-layer norms for flagged prompts.
[30:10] Priya: we ran a small experiment: AWQ 4-bit improved memory by 45% but we saw a 2% accuracy hit on long-form summarization. is that fixable?
[30:20] Diego: likely yes — keep last n layers at fp16 or 8-bit, retune calibration, sometimes a tiny bias compensation term reduces systematic shift.
[32:00] Asha: let's discuss pilot timeline — ideally start within 2 weeks.
[32:06] Samira: feasible — Diego, can you prepare artifacts this week?
[32:10] Diego: yes, i'll produce INT8 and AWQ builds and a benchmark harness (upload link).
[32:16] Samira: i'll send the sheet and security docs.
[32:19] Asha: Priya/Markus will stand up the dev VPC tests.
[32:23] Priya: yep.
[32:26] [pause]
[40:00] Diego: one more micro-optimization: kernel selection for short vs long seqs. some kernels optimize for short context with fused attention; quantized kernels sometimes disable fusion leading to small perf regressions on short prompts. we recommend toggling kernel hints per workload distribution.
[40:22] Markus: that's interesting — we have a mix of short and very long. how are hints configured?
[40:28] Diego: via runtime config or per-route config in Redwood console. we can suggest defaults after we see traces.
[41:00] Samira: ok i'll capture that in the follow-up doc.
[41:05] Asha: last question: if pilot succeeds, can we automate continuous quantization for new model versions?
[41:12] Diego: yes — you can commit calibration configs to CI, run quant conversion on model artifact ingestion, run delta-evals, and gate promotion based on thresholds. Redwood supports hooks into your CI.
[41:27] Priya: nice.
[41:30] Samira: recap quick: Diego produces quant builds and harness; Samira shares docs and sheet; Zenith runs dev VPC tests; follow-up in one week.
[41:40] Asha: good recap, thanks.
[41:45] Markus: few legal/security asks before we share anything sensitive — can you forward SOC2 and KMS integrations notes?
[41:52] Samira: yes, will attach SOC2 summary and notes on KMS/HSM and per-route encryption.
[41:58] Priya: what's the expected data movement for the benchmark? we prefer metrics only.
[42:03] Diego: you can run the harness in your VPC; we only need aggregated metrics and traces, not raw prompt text.
[42:12] Asha: perfect. thanks everyone.
[42:16] Samira: any final Qs?
[42:18] Priya: no, we're good.
[42:20] Samira: great — next steps as discussed, i'll schedule follow-up. thanks all.
[42:27] Endcall notes: meeting lasted 53m per platform. Attachments: AWQ_vs_GPTQ_benchmark_sheet (link), Redwood_security_summary (link), quant_artifacts (to be uploaded).
